newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian financiers urge tough line on unions.
newsitem.headline: Colombian financiers urge tough line on unions.

text.p: Colombia should press ahead with a planned wave of privatizations in order to break the backbone of union power, an influential financiers group said in a report Sunday.

The National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF) also urged the government to place vital supplies, such as fuel and gasoline, under the control of the armed forces to prevent shortages during the on-going public sector workers' national strike, now in its sixth day.
Talks aimed at resolving the work stoppage by an estimated 800,000 state workers broke down early Friday and did not resume, as initially expected, over the weekend.

"The only response to the pressures of a group of state employees should be an intensification of the privatization process and greater competition in the supply of basic services," ANIF said in its weekly report.
"Society cannot be subject to the threats of monopolies controlled by small groups of people who do not hesitate in putting the economy's back against the wall," it added.

The state workers are pressing for a 21.5 percent pay hike. They are also demanding an end to the planned sell-off of a number of regional and national industries, which the government currently owns or in which it has a part stake, and an overhaul of what they say is a repressive labor code.
As part of its austerity drive to rein in a yawning fiscal deficit the government offered public sector workers a weighted 13.5 percent pay rise -- below the 1996 inflation rate of 21.6 percent.
In the course of negotiations with union representatives it has refused to back down on privatization plans -- one of the cornerstones of President Ernesto Samper's neoliberal economic policy.
Labor leaders and the government have issued conflicting reports on the impact of the strike.

Samper said only 10 percent of public sector employees had heeded the strike call while union bosses said the stoppage was "total" and had severely disrupted key economic and social sectors, including telecommunications, education and all but emergency health care.
The strike seems set to bite harder this week as Colombia's main oil workers' union threatens to step up industrial action.
The deadline for an agreement between the 7,000-strong USO union and the state-run oil company Ecopetrol on a new collective contract which expires Monday.
USO leader Hernando Hernndez said if no deal emerged the union could move to paralyze all oil activities.

The USO has been in the forefront of the national, indefinite strike since it started at midnight last Monday but has so far permitted non-unionized administrative employees to run production and refining operations.

In anticipation of possible USO attempts to shut down the oil industry, ANIF urged in its report: "It is necessary to create strategic reserves of gasoline and other fuel and these should be amanged by organizations other than Ecopetrol...in other countries for example these are controlled by the armed forces."
